body:
> Found operating this board on 2026-09-01, on WSL2 (Linux 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, node v24.20.0).
> `hkb up --serve` had started both processes 30 minutes earlier and they were still running.

## Why

`pidFileStale` (`src/model.js:1164`) decides whether a pid file survived a reboot by arithmetic:
`mtime < now - os.uptime() * 1000 - 5_000`. The reasoning is sound — a file written before this machine booted
cannot name a live process of ours — but it assumes the wall clock and `os.uptime()` stay in step for the life of
the machine. **On WSL2 they do not.** The VM's clock is resynced against the Windows host across suspend/resume
while `/proc/uptime` keeps its own count, so the derived boot instant walks forward and eventually crosses pid
files written earlier in the same session.

Measured here, with both processes alive (`ps` shows pid 1101 `dispatch --loop 60` and pid 1122 `serve`, 32
minutes elapsed):

```
os.uptime()            2054.62 s
derived boot           2026-09-01T17:42:32Z
.kanban/dispatch.pid   2026-09-01T17:32:37Z   ← written by hkb, 10 min "before boot"
stale?                 true
```

```
$ hkb up --status
dispatch stopped (pid file predates this boot — hkb up replaces it)
serve stopped (pid file predates this boot — hkb up replaces it)
```

The failure is not cosmetic. `startProcess` only stands down when the claim is believed — `src/up.js:81`,
`if (!stale && current && current !== pid && pidAlive(current)) return false` — so with `stale` true, **`hkb up`
spawns a second dispatcher against a board that already has one**, which is the double-claim the pid file exists
to prevent and which the skill promises cannot happen ("safe to type twice"). The same read gates the
dispatcher's own singleton lock (`src/dispatch.js:1026`) and the server's claim (`src/serve.js:125`), and
`hkb doctor` reports `no dispatcher running` (`src/doctor.js:138`) while the loop is ticking.

This is the mirror of #202, which guards the *false-live* direction (a pid reused after a reboot). Both want the
same thing: a claim that identifies the process, not just a number and a timestamp. Worth deciding the two
together.

## What

Do not widen `PID_BOOT_SLACK_MS` — the skew here is ten minutes and unbounded, and a slack big enough to cover it
would defeat the guard it belongs to.

- **Prefer a real boot instant over a derived one.** `/proc/stat`'s `btime` is a fixed epoch second written at
  boot and does not drift with the clock; read it when it exists and fall back to `os.uptime()` where it does
  not (macOS: `kern.boottime`; otherwise the arithmetic). Note that on the machine above `btime` agreed with
  `os.uptime()`, so this alone may not be the fix — verify on WSL2 before building on it.
- **Corroborate before declaring a claim dead.** Staleness is currently a verdict from one timestamp. A pid file
  whose pid is alive *and* whose `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` names our own `hkb dispatch --loop` / `hkb serve` for this
  root is our process, whatever the arithmetic says — cheap, zero-dependency, and it settles #202's direction too
  (a stranger that inherited the pid will not match). Where `/proc` is absent, keep the timestamp verdict.
- **Never let a stale verdict alone authorise a spawn.** Whatever the rule becomes, `hkb up` must check liveness
  before starting a rival: today a wrong `stale` is a silent second dispatcher, and the whole point of the pid
  file is that this cannot happen. Failing closed here costs a manual `hkb down`; failing open costs
  double-claimed cards.
- Keep the decision a pure function in `src/model.js` with the boot/`/proc` reads injected, per the layout rule.

## Done when

- [ ] A pid file written by the current `hkb up`, on a machine whose clock has jumped forward relative to
      `os.uptime()`, is not reported stale — with a unit test that fakes exactly that skew.
- [ ] `hkb up --status` and `hkb doctor` report the running dispatcher and server on WSL2.
- [ ] `hkb up` never spawns a second dispatcher while one is alive, on any path through the staleness check.
- [ ] A genuinely post-reboot pid file naming a reused pid is still refused (the #202 direction does not regress).
- [ ] `npm run lint && npm test` pass; the wiki page covering `hkb up` / process state is updated.
goal: A pid file written by the running hkb up is never reported stale when the wall clock drifts against os.uptime (WSL2); up --status and doctor see the live processes; hkb up cannot spawn a second dispatcher while one is alive; the post-reboot reused-pid case still fails closed
title: hkb up --status calls a live dispatcher stopped on WSL2, and hkb up would then start a second one
